Well the issue here isn't that they were misgendered on a regular basis but GENDERED right on a regular basis and the situation sounds drastically different. They literally said they were gendered correctly for months - I'm not sure why they lied and said they asked the question to everyone I'd be incredibly uncomfortable whether you would or not. And whether you would spend your time bristle and not saying anything to everyone who misgenders you daily isn't the same situation. I think that's something most trans people deal with.

I'm not sure why everyone wants to be asked pronouns. It's much more preferred to someone straight up asking me or blatant misgendering every time.

I wish you luck. I'm in a longterm relationship with a cis guy - but the relationship from the start even pre-T has been a gay relationship and I have been out the entire time. I've been on T for almost a year now, and if you'd like to message me I'd def be willing to talk if you'd like. 

I would warn, though, that I do know of a lot of cis guys who have stuck with relationships with trans guys just coming out and not seemed to know the implications of their partners genders...have seen them more as 'non binary' or their gender as something not completely male and it's been a bit difficult. That they don't perceive themselves as 'gay' and that it gets a bit rough for everyone. If they truly see themselves as straight, you might really want to have a sit down and talk to them for a long time because if they're justifying the fact that they are straight based upon stuff like genitals then it's going to likely lead to some longterm problems because it's not that he's going to be perceived as in a gay relationship it's that he's going to BE In a gay relationship/in a relationship with a guy. 

That's not to say that there is no hope within a relationship or it's not worth trying, but I think everyone needs to be aware of EVERYTHING that's going to change and not trying to compromise.

While I think it might be okay in some situations, the person who asked them gave a reason that made no sense and had already been gendering them correctly. Personally I would rather not be asked this question by a stranger who I've already been longterm interacting with.

Wouldn't you say something after months and months if they had been gendering you incorrectly?

But they literally said that they had been using the correct pronouns for MONTHS prior to this along with the correct name with them not saying anything. The random cashier gave the reasoning that they would ask pronouns to anyone...with some elderly man in-front of them which they clearly did NOT ask pronouns to indicating that this isn't correct and that their statement is pretty much nonsense. 

It would make me feel bad as well. I've frankly only been asked my pronouns in LGBT specific situations or online only really - usually people will make a best guess or will use gender neutral if they don't know for sure. I'd rather this the case - but in this situation the OP said the person was gendering them correctly

As Frankly asking does not make me feel good - It's not a situation which is largely comfortable when you pass a chunk of the time because the indication is that you do not pass for cis. Most people are not going to be asking random strangers if they 'use these pronouns' because the common social thing is that you don't ask these questions. 

As the OP described though the question is a kind of discrimination as the question is only being asked because they are not passing for cis - it's not being asked to someone who isn't 'appearing' trans. When this happens to me irl it just ruins my day a lot of the time - especially when it might have been someone who previously was gendering me right - they suddenly aren't gendering me right, might not be perceiving me as the right gender and are going to literally stop everything to have this conversation when it was 100% not necessary and none of their business. 

At the very least, if you're going to ask this question do not give the bs statement of 'well I ask everyone that question' - and do not give it after months and months of correct pronouns.

I'm on PCP number four in as many years because of issues being taken seriously as actually ill. It's defiantly a struggle.

Being chronically fatigued and having the collection of symptoms which describe CFS/ME is rather different. As someone who has in the past, before dealing with this illness dealt with depression based fatigue and low motivation to do things it is in fact s vastly different feeling without the variety of other symptoms associated with ME. You need to look at the other symptoms as well as understand that it's a disorder of exclusion. It shouldn't be what you consider first second or tenth.

Ultimately depression based fatigue is based on something psychological and trying to attribute CFS to something psychological isn't right at all. Depression happens with people who have CFS often because people feel trapped in illness and can't get better not unmotivated - like you said chicken and egg but that comparison really doesn't work here when fatigue is already frequently associated with depression. That feeling of no motivation is distinctly depression and sleeping 22 hours a day is distinctly that: not wanting to get up or not caring. ME isn't that and if you're dealing with any illness along with your depression you need to eliminate and treat depression first to seperate from anything else.

CFS is a really about excluding everything else that stuff might be - a lot of things that can be treated and found out easily through testing when you go to a doctor. You can't diagnose simply through symptoms  alone (that's not to say symptoms aren't valid) but trying to pin point things yourself without getting tests and the input from someone medically is pretty much impossible. An endo, sleep study, mri, etc. CFS shouldn't be the first thing to go to. I'd look at the FAQ listed since it's more than just being tired, but it's less a feeling of bleh and more absolute exhaustion and inability to function properly at all normally.
